segments.text: Let's talk about teamwork. Now, you might think that when more people work on a task, the group naturally becomes more productive. Well, believe it or not, research suggests the opposite can happen.

In the early 1900s, an engineer named Max Ringelmann asked people to pull on a rope, first alone and then in groups. He expected the total force to increase with every added person. Instead, each person pulled a little less hard as the group grew. Psychologists now call this effect social loafing.

Why does it happen? Partly because individual effort becomes harder to see in a crowd. People think, 'Nobody will notice if I relax a little.' Fortunately, the effect is not inevitable. When each member has a clear, visible responsibility, social loafing nearly disappears. So the next time you work on a group project, don't just divide the topic. Assign names to specific tasks.
